member.name: T:FinanceSentry.Infrastructure.Auditing.AuditedWriteSaveChangesInterceptor
member.summary:
Puts every save of an entity on the audit trail, once per row, before the save commits: no write of declared profile data goes unrecorded, and the handler that makes it does not have to remember to. Records the entity's resource type, its id and the NAMES of the fields it wrote - for a new row every field, for an edit the fields whose value changed, for a delete none. It never reads a value out of the entity.
A Modified row with no changed field (a re-save, or a key rotation rewriting ciphertext) records nothing: it wrote no new fact. Bookkeeping columns (CreatedAt, UpdatedAt) are not fields of the profile.
The audit row is written first, in its own context, so a failed audit stops the write. The reverse failure - the audit row is stored and the write then fails - leaves a trail entry for an attempted write, which is the safe side.

member.name: T:FinanceSentry.Infrastructure.Encryption.CredentialEncryptionService
member.summary:
AES-256-GCM credential encryption service.
Security properties: - AES-256-GCM provides authenticated encryption (confidentiality + integrity). - Each call to Encrypt() generates a fresh 12-byte IV — never reuse an IV. - The 16-byte authentication tag is verified on Decrypt(); tampered data is rejected. - Key is derived from a master key stored in environment config (never in source code). - Key versioning enables rotation: old encrypted credentials retain their key version so they can still be decrypted after rotation.
SC-007: Encrypt + Decrypt cycle must complete within 50ms on average.

member.name: T:FinanceSentry.Infrastructure.Encryption.EncryptedField
member.summary:
The stored form of one field-encrypted value: a single text column holding v{keyVersion}.{iv}.{tag}.{ciphertext}, the last three base64. The key version travels with the value, so a row stays readable after the current key moves on, and rotation can find the rows still on an older key without decrypting them.
This is the primitive for declared profile data (income, goals, career amounts), stored as text rather than as the byte[] columns the provider credentials use: OwnedRowExporter drops every byte[] column, so a declared amount stored the way a credential is would vanish from the person's data download. Here the entity property stays plaintext in code; the converter encrypts on write and decrypts on read, and the export writes the decrypted value because the property is not a secret to its owner.
An empty string is stored as the empty string: that it is empty is not a secret, and AES-GCM over zero bytes is refused by .

member.name: T:FinanceSentry.Infrastructure.Encryption.EncryptionOptionsValidator
member.summary:
Startup validation for (issue #493).
The service used to inject whenever Encryption:Keys was empty. No key was configured in production, so every stored bank credential was AES-GCM-encrypted under a key committed to a public repository — and nothing said so. Two rules replace that silence:
Outside Development, an unconfigured or disclosed key is a startup failure. Paired with ValidateOnStart() the process refuses to come up, rather than serving traffic and failing at the first credential read.
In Development the fallback survives so a local checkout still runs — but it is announced at Warning level on every boot. The disclosed key is a development convenience and is never again reachable anywhere else.
Rule 1 covers the key arriving from ANY source, not just the removed fallback: pasting the disclosed value into a production appsettings or env var is the same disclosure, so it is refused on its value rather than on where it came from.

member.name: T:FinanceSentry.Infrastructure.Encryption.ICredentialRotationTarget
member.summary:
One store of encrypted credentials that key rotation must migrate (issue #493).
Rotation exists because the disclosed fallback key was in use in production: removing the fallback stops NEW credentials being written under it, but every row already written stays readable by anyone with the repository until it is re-encrypted. A store that holds encrypted credentials and does not implement this interface is silently left on the old key, so a new credential store must add an implementation in the same change that adds the store.
Contract for implementers:
Idempotent. Select only rows whose key version differs from the target; a second run over an already-rotated store does nothing and returns 0.
Atomic per row. Persist each row's new ciphertext, IV, auth tag and key version together. A row is never left with a new ciphertext and an old version (undecryptable) or an old ciphertext and a new version (decryptable only by accident).
Fail loud. A row that cannot be decrypted is a real problem — a wrong key or tampered data — and must surface, not be skipped.

member.name: T:FinanceSentry.Infrastructure.Observability.Hangfire.HangfireManualRequeueDetectionFilter
member.summary:
Marks an operator-initiated Hangfire dashboard Requeue for (#616 follow-up): a state-election signal the requeue itself produces, not an inference from job age. It fires when a job is elected into straight from a state only a manual action reaches from there — , , — or from a that already carries a positive RetryCount, i.e. a retry-scheduled state an operator jumped ahead of its backoff.
AutomaticRetryAttribute never elects itself: on a failure under its attempt budget it elects for the next attempt, and once the budget is exhausted it leaves the job in . So any election into from one of the states above is never its doing — this filter does not need to identify "who" produced the election beyond ruling that out structurally.
A plain with no RetryCount is deliberately excluded: that is an ad-hoc delayed job reaching its scheduled time for the first time, still a first attempt, and must keep today's parent-child behaviour.

member.name: T:FinanceSentry.Infrastructure.Observability.Hangfire.HangfireTracingFilter
member.summary:
Propagates trace context across the Hangfire queue boundary (spec 023 amendment, #616): on enqueue () it stores the ambient 's W3C traceparent/tracestate as job parameters — never the whole or Baggage, neither of which survives the serialize/deserialize round trip through job storage. On execution () it starts an from FinanceSentry.Hangfire: a child of the stored context for the first attempt of an ad-hoc enqueue, or an to it for a recurring trigger, every automatic retry, and every manual requeue. A thrown job exception marks the activity before it closes.
Why retries link instead of parent. "One trace per request" holds only for the first attempt. Hangfire's automatic retry backs off between attempts, so a retry can run minutes or hours after the request span closed; parenting it would stretch the request's trace across that gap and make a fast request look like an hours-long one. The failure that caused the retry is an operational event in its own right, so each retry gets its own root trace, keeps a link back to the originating request, and carries hangfire.job_id + hangfire.retry_count tags so all attempts of one job can still be grouped from either end.
Manual requeue gets the same treatment. An operator's dashboard Requeue is not an automatic retry — AutomaticRetryAttribute never writes RetryCount for it, so keying on that counter alone would re-parent the job onto the original request's trace however much later the requeue happens (a week-old trace gaining a fresh span), and would do so inconsistently: a job declared with Attempts = 0 is always parented, while one whose automatic retries already ran out stays linked purely because the stale counter is still positive. closes that gap with a signal the requeue itself produces — a state-election filter, not job age — and records ; this filter treats that marker exactly like RetryCount > 0 and then clears it so a later automatic retry of the requeued run follows the ordinary retry rule.
